raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the first clinically successful angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), pairing valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade with sacubitril, a prodrug converted to the neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657. The rationale is biologically attractive: neprilysin inhibition augments natriuretic peptides and other vasoactive substrates, increasing cyclic guanosine monophosphate signaling, natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic pathways, while angiotensin receptor blockade prevents maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation that might otherwise be amplified by neprilysin inhibition [1]. Pharmacokinetic studies show rapid absorption and predictable exposure to sacubitrilat and valsartan, supporting twice-daily dosing and titration in clinical practice [2].

Early evidence came from PARAMOUNT, in which LCZ696 reduced NT-proBNP more than valsartan in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), suggesting hemodynamic or wall-stress benefit [3]. The pivotal advance was PARADIGM-HF, which randomized patients with chronic symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril and demonstrated significant reductions in cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalization, and all-cause mortality [4]. Secondary analyses indicated less clinical progression among survivors [5], preserved efficacy and acceptable safety across age groups [6], more frequent loop-diuretic dose reduction [7], modest improvements in glycemic control among patients with diabetes [8], slower renal-function decline in patients with diabetes [9], and a characteristic biomarker profile in which NT-proBNP falls while BNP may rise because BNP is a neprilysin substrate [10].

Subsequent studies addressed initiation. PIONEER-HF showed that, after hemodynamic stabilization during hospitalization for acute decompensated HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan reduced NT-proBNP more than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [11]. A mechanistic PIONEER-HF substudy showed early reductions in high-sensitivity troponin T and soluble ST2 and increases in urinary cyclic GMP, supporting rapid effects on myocardial injury and wall stress [12]. TRANSITION demonstrated feasibility of starting treatment before discharge or soon after discharge [13], while TITRATION informed practical up-titration, especially for patients previously receiving low-dose or no renin–angiotensin system inhibition [14].

Mechanistic remodeling data complement outcome trials. PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reduction after sacubitril/valsartan initiation with reverse remodeling, including improved ejection fraction and reduced ventricular and atrial volumes [15]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant reduction in aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril, but it did show favorable changes in several echocardiographic remodeling measures [16]. Patient-centered data from PROVE-HF also suggested improved health status after initiation [17]. In contrast, the LIFE trial in advanced HFrEF did not show significant benefit of sacubitril/valsartan over valsartan on NT-proBNP area under the curve, emphasizing that tolerability and efficacy may be attenuated in stage D disease [18].

Evidence across higher ejection fractions is more nuanced. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death in HFpEF [19]. However, prespecified and post hoc analyses suggested greater benefit in women [20] and in patients with ejection fraction below the normal range [21]. Renal analyses in PARAGON-HF suggested fewer adverse renal outcomes versus valsartan [22], and diuretic analyses showed fewer new loop-diuretic initiations [23]. PARALLAX confirmed a significant NT-proBNP reduction in patients with ejection fraction above 40%, but without improvement in 6-minute walk distance [24]. PARAGLIDE-HF extended biomarker evidence to patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction after a recent worsening heart-failure event [25].

Safety considerations are central. Sacubitril/valsartan causes more hypotension than enalapril in some settings but often less hyperkalemia or renal impairment; it must not be combined with an ACE inhibitor and requires a 36-hour washout to reduce angioedema risk. Experience with omapatrilat, a vasopeptidase inhibitor combining ACE and neprilysin inhibition, highlighted unacceptable angioedema risk and helped shape the ARB-based ARNI strategy [26]. PARADISE-MI did not establish superiority over ramipril after acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced ejection fraction, pulmonary congestion, or both, so routine post-MI replacement of ACE inhibition remains unproven [27].

Guidelines now position sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, preferably replacing ACE inhibitors or ARBs when feasible, and as a consideration in selected patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, particularly those near the lower end of the ejection-fraction spectrum [28], [29]. Practical implementation requires attention to blood pressure, renal function, potassium, prior ACE-inhibitor exposure, cost, and adherence; expert guidance supports starting at lower doses in vulnerable patients and titrating toward 97/103 mg twice daily as tolerated [30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan is a cornerstone of modern HFrEF therapy, with compelling mortality and hospitalization benefits, rapid biomarker and remodeling effects, and a more selective but evolving role in heart failure with ejection fraction above 40%.
